episodes.text: Voluntarily retired from a stable government military-engineering post in 1844 to pursue writing full-time, before any publication track record existed.

By his own later account in letters, was not a dedicated or brilliant student at the Military Engineering Academy and instead sustained deep, self-directed interest in literature (Schiller, Homer) throughout, diverging from the assigned technical curriculum.
On sudden critical acclaim for his first novel Poor Folk (age 24), wrote to his brother Mikhail in open elation: "I have a brilliant future before me, brother!"

After his very next work (The Double) was received coolly -- including by Belinsky, the same critic who had championed him months before -- continued producing new work across markedly different genres and forms in rapid succession (1846-1849) rather than retreating to his previously successful mode.
Voluntarily joined the Petrashevsky Circle in 1847, a politically dangerous discussion group critical of serfdom/autocracy, under a regime known to suppress dissent.

Underwent an 8-month pre-trial imprisonment followed by a staged mock execution (December 1849) -- kneeling, ritual sword-breaking, tied to a post, blindfolded -- before a last-second announced reprieve; unknown to the prisoners, the commutation had already been decided the day before as deliberate psychological terror.

In a letter to his brother written hours after the reprieve, described an intensified will-to-live and religious/existential reframing ("Life is a gift, life is happiness... I am living again!") rather than despair, paralysis, or anger at his captors.

Served four years of hard labor among ordinary criminal convicts, not political prisoners, as a nobleman by birth; reportedly despised and distrusted by most of the convicts around him, requiring adaptation to sustained social hostility on top of the physical hardship of the labor itself.

Kept ongoing observational notes on convicts' speech, arguments, and behavior during imprisonment despite restrictive conditions (only a New Testament permitted), converting this material years later into published work (Notes from the House of the Dead, serialized 1860-62).

Explicitly revised his own prior simple/binary moral categories after direct field observation in the labor camp, later writing he was astonished by convicts' capacity for murder "without the slightest change in conscience" while also finding "good and decent individuals" among them.

Co-founded and co-edited the literary/political journal Vremya with brother Mikhail, jointly managing deadlines, censorship pressure, and business operations; after its suppression by authorities, co-founded a successor journal, Epokha.

On his brother Mikhail's sudden death (1864), voluntarily assumed personal responsibility for roughly 20,000-25,000 rubles of his brother's business debt plus ongoing support of his own stepson and younger brother, ultimately declaring personal bankruptcy rather than disclaiming the obligation.

Wrote and published the philosophical novella Notes from Underground (1864), developing an anti-rationalist/anti-utopian argument that people "desire freedom more than happiness," composed concurrently with his most acute personal financial and emotional crisis.

Facing a punitive publishing contract (deliver an entirely new novel within roughly a month or forfeit all publishing rights to existing and future work for nine years), hired a stenographer and dictated a full novel (The Gambler) to the deadline, then accepted her practical suggestion to file the manuscript with a notary when the publisher's office turned out to be closed -- filed roughly two hours before the deadline and later upheld by courts.

His new wife Anna's contemporaneous 1867 diary records a repeating pattern of sharp quarrels within the marriage ("Fyodor got into a terrible rage," "completely lost his temper" after rude restaurant service) followed by quick reconciliation and affectionate repair within the same day or period -- a first-person eyewitness account by the person who observed it daily.

During the gambling addiction's most acute phase abroad (1867-1871), letters to Anna document a repeating cycle -- confession of a loss, plea for forgiveness, promise never to repeat, then recurrence -- while Anna, pregnant, repeatedly pawned her own possessions to fund him or cover basic costs after his losses.

The gambling addiction had a specific, dated hard stop -- April 24, 1871, a final loss at the Wiesbaden casino recorded as the last time he ever gambled -- an abrupt, durable behavior change after roughly a decade of repeated relapse, rather than a gradual fade.

Sustained major, demanding long-form creative work (Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, The Possessed) in direct parallel with, not sequentially after, his acute financial crisis and gambling addiction abroad.

Over roughly a decade from the early 1870s, progressively ceded real financial and business authority (contract negotiation, pricing, publishing operations) to Anna, explicitly writing to her in 1876 "everything is in your power alone... I so highly value and trust in your mind" -- a direct reversal of the prior decade's pattern of exclusively self-directed financial decisions that had produced chronic crisis.

Independently wrote, edited, and published a personal monthly periodical (A Writer's Diary, from 1876) largely alone -- suspending work on The Brothers Karamazov to sustain it -- and engaged in direct, sustained correspondence with lay readers who wrote in response to specific pieces.

Sustained a long-running public feud with fellow novelist Ivan Turgenev rooted in explicit ideological disagreement, including years of mutual public mockery -- yet, under acute financial pressure after a gambling loss, directly asked Turgenev for a loan, received half the amount requested, and repaid the debt eleven years later despite the ongoing personal antagonism.

Delivered a major public speech at the Pushkin monument unveiling (June 1880) that reportedly moved the audience to tears and, per some accounts, briefly reconciled rival Slavophile and Westernizer factions in the room, though other accounts note initial rejection by some younger radical listeners.

Repeatedly and directly converted real contemporary events into major fiction across his whole career at very different time lags -- a courier's roadside cruelty witnessed as a teenager (reused decades later in two novels), a newspaper account of a seamstress's suicide (turned into The Meek One within the same publication cycle), and the 1869 Nechaev-circle murder (turned into The Possessed) -- a sustained pattern of converting observed reality into literary material rather than working purely from invention.
